Learning to Walk in Handan: Why Can Learning from Others Cost Us What We Already Know?
A young man heard that the people of Handan walked gracefully, and went there to learn.
He wanted to walk as they did.
But before mastering the new steps, he lost his original way of walking.
In the end, he could not walk home normally. He had to crawl away.
The fable is often used to mock blind imitation:
Failing to learn someone else's skills and losing your own in the process.
There is sense in that lesson.
But concluding “Don't imitate others; just stay yourself” would rush the story again.
Because learning is never entirely free of imitation.
Children learning language, beginners practicing a craft, and people entering unfamiliar environments all first watch what others do, then try to repeat it.
The problem is not that he learns from others.
The question is:
**Is he acquiring a new ability to walk, or merely trying to look like someone from another place?**
Walking is an interesting ability.
Once we become proficient, we hardly need to think through each step.
How the foot lands, how the body balances, and how speed is adjusted become automatic through long experience.
Changing such an ability requires more than remembering a few outward poses.
New movements have to find their way into the body.
They must coordinate with balance, ground, rhythm, and a particular purpose, finally becoming a way of moving that remains usable under different conditions.
If a learner copies only the visible shape without developing the ability that supports it, what they learn is closer to a performance.
In front of the teacher, the resemblance may be convincing.
On another road, at another speed, or on uneven ground, the movements cease to work.
Real ability includes more than “looking the same.” It includes being able to keep accomplishing something when conditions change.
The young man in Handan may have mistaken posture for ability too soon.
In correcting every old movement, he begins to distrust his own body before it has truly mastered the new method. The old route is prohibited; the new one cannot yet bear weight.
The force of “crawling home” is more than its comedy.
It shows that the learning process left him nowhere to stand, even temporarily.
Why would someone discard an old ability completely before the new one has formed?
Sometimes an old ability really does obstruct new learning.

An established habit automatically gets there first. Without temporarily slowing it down, taking it apart, or even suspending it, a different movement is hard to build. Learning therefore often includes an unstable period: the familiar way no longer feels easy, and the new way is not yet natural.
This loss of balance does not make learning a mistake.
No one can guarantee that growth will always be smooth.
If fear of temporary regression makes us unwilling ever to loosen our grip on old methods, we can only become increasingly proficient within familiar bounds.
The fable cannot therefore prove:
The old way of walking is the truest, and every change in oneself is betrayal.
The real question is whether learning leaves room for correction and return.
When a new method fails, can someone use an old ability that still works?
Can they bring the useful parts of the old method into the new?
Can they adjust to their own body and problem, rather than measuring everything by “Do I look like someone from Handan?”
Can they admit they have not yet learned, rather than keep pretending the old ability is inferior to protect a new identity?
The young man's failure lies in more than imitation.
It also lies in learning being written as a complete replacement:
Before becoming a new self, you must first reject your old self.
This kind of learning is common enough.
Someone enters a new professional environment and learns its more precise language, but gradually becomes afraid to explain a problem in their own words.
A creator falls in love with a predecessor's style. The work looks increasingly similar, but the questions that genuinely troubled the creator no longer appear.
Someone rapidly adopts every way of speaking and judging in a new group to fit in. After leaving, they no longer know which opinions they are still willing to stand behind.
On the surface, all these changes look like progress.
The language is more professional, the work more mature, the conduct more fitting.
But if a new ability can exist only through continued imitation and outside confirmation, it has not truly become the learner's ability.
After truly learning, someone can not only reproduce an answer but know when not to use it; not only take the same steps but adjust them on different roads.
An ability becomes one's own not by forgetting its source, but by becoming able to answer one's own questions.
Nor is “one's own way” something complete at birth and incapable of change.
The young man's original steps were simply the steps he already knew, not necessarily the best, nor enough to take him everywhere.
If we read the fable as “Nothing foreign fits; staying unchanged is safest,” we turn learning itself into a danger.
We learn precisely because others have abilities we have not yet developed.
A good teacher, a mature tradition, or an unfamiliar way of life can genuinely expand what someone is able to do.
The key is not rejecting outside influence, but how that influence is eventually reorganized within us.
We can begin by copying.
We can allow our movements to be awkward for a while.
We can spend a period concentrating on standards others provide.
But learning cannot remain forever at “What would someone else do?”
Sooner or later, it has to return to:
What problem am I facing now?
What can this ability accomplish here?
What are its limits?
When the standard conflicts with reality, can I make my own adjustments?
If not, the learner has merely imported an external answer, without acquiring the ability to produce answers.
The original context in the Zhuangzi gives this short fable another layer of weight.
It is not a stand-alone joke about a city. It appears in an admonition about the limits of understanding.

Gongsun Long brings his familiar framework of debate and knowledge to language far beyond its scale. Through the well frog, looking through a tube, and learning to walk in Handan, Wei Mou warns him: if he insists on measuring things by existing abilities while rushing to imitate something greater, he may neither truly understand the new material nor retain the foundation that previously worked.
This does not ask Gongsun Long to stop learning.
Quite the contrary: it asks him first to see the limits of his current method.
Knowing one's limits is not self-belittlement.
Only by knowing where we stand can we truly move elsewhere.
If we pretend from the outset to stand where the people of Handan stand, learning becomes merely copying poses.
Imitation is especially likely to become attached to identity.
The young man may want more than a new movement.
He may want to become “the kind of person people in Handan are.”
Once the new method is tied to a higher identity, retaining an old ability becomes shameful.
Even if his old walk can still take him safely home, he may refuse to use it because it seems to admit he has not become the new person he imagined.
That shame makes learning inflexible.
We stop asking which method is useful now and ask only which proves we belong to a higher rank.
Ability becomes subordinate to image.
Sometimes we would rather crawl than take a few steps in the old way again.
Crawling can be explained as a cost of learning. The old walk feels like a failure of identity.
Real growth need not protect a new identity this way.
It lets us say:
I am learning, but I have not learned it yet.
This part is useful to me; that part does not fit my conditions.
I can return to the old method temporarily, and I can keep making changes.
These statements lack grandeur, but they keep ability in the service of action rather than proof that “I have changed.”
Learning from others carries another danger within the relationship.
If teachers or models treat their own form as the only correct answer, they will interpret a learner's differences as shortcomings.
A different stride is not standard enough.
A different rhythm means insufficient effort.
Using the ability for a different purpose means not truly understanding it.
Eventually, learning is judged successful only if the student increasingly resembles the teacher.
Such teaching can produce great similarity without necessarily producing stronger judgment or action.
Real teaching should know that it is handing on an ability, not producing a copy.
Once students learn, they may use the ability somewhere the teacher never anticipated, or change the teacher's method.
If teaching counts as successful only while students forever retain the teacher's shape, it is still cultivating dependence.
The story does not say whether the people of Handan actually demanded this of the young man.
So the teachers cannot be given all the blame.
But the fable shows that learners can actively turn other people into standards they must copy.
How can we judge whether learning has really taken place?
We can look at results, but not only results.
We can also ask:
Can the learner continue without the demonstration?
Can they adjust when conditions change?
Faced with a new problem, can they explain why they act this way?
When a method proves unsuitable, can they revise it without feeling they have failed as a whole person?
Do they have more possibilities for action than before, or only one correct pose they must maintain?
Good learning gives someone more ways to walk.
Even if they finally choose one, they know it is a choice, not the only way they can stand.
Bad learning may close off the old route, then allow the new one to exist only under someone else's gaze.
The young man's crawling return is an exaggerated, sharp ending.
It makes failed imitation visible.
But what deserves to stay with us is not laughter at him.
Someone willing to leave the familiar and try an unfamiliar ability already takes the risk of failure. If we merely mock him, we shrink the story to “Don't risk changing.”
The better questions are:
Why did he not stop while he could still walk?
Why did the old ability lose permission to be used before the new one had formed?
Why must learning mean becoming someone else completely, rather than letting another's ability acquire a new shape within oneself?
These questions come closer to growth than “Do not imitate.”
Because real learning has never meant rejecting others.
It means allowing others to change us without permanently handing the source of our actions over to an external model.
The walk of Handan can be a gift.
That gift truly arrives only when the young man can finally use it to walk his own road.
If, at the end of learning, he merely looks more like someone from Handan but can no longer take his next step from his own resources, he has not gained a new ability to walk.
Only a pose that must constantly be proved.

*Textual basis: the short fable of “a youth of Shouling learning to walk in Handan,” in Wei Mou's admonition to Gongsun Long in the Zhuangzi, “Autumn Floods.” The original emphasizes that he “had not acquired that country's skill, yet lost his former way of walking, and could only crawl home.” This essay does not reduce the tale to opposition to imitation. It distinguishes outward posture, genuine ability, temporary imbalance during learning, and whether the learner can continue using a new ability independently after leaving the model behind.*
